item.text: {"text":"Recent work cautions against equating sequence sensitivity with useful sequence modeling. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) quantify excessive recency emphasis and report improvements after mitigation in their experiments. [Liu et al. (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) show that random history shuffling conflates user behavior with item availability; their constrained shuffle prevents interactions preceding an item’s first observed appearance. [Spotify Research (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) reports pairwise transition models outperforming both tested Transformers on four of five benchmarks, motivating separate checks for last-item dependence, additive historical evidence, and joint contextual effects.\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: use paired interventions through log2feats/predict_score on fixed users and candidates. Shuffle only nonpadding prefix items while preserving the last item, length, and item multiset; compare recent versus older deletions matched by count; distinguish deletion with fixed position holes from compacted histories to expose position effects. Probe repetition by replacing an older item with an existing history item, paired with a training-popularity-matched replacement control. Compare full-history and last-item-only scores, ranking changes, top-10 overlap, and association with training interaction frequency. These measure behavioral dependence, not causal recommendation gains; assess usefulness separately with unchanged validation HR@10. Bound users, batches, and perturbations; use inference mode, isolate diagnostic random generators, and restore every module’s prior training state. Treat these implementation controls as proposed safeguards, not a standardized protocol established by the cited papers."}
